(Phone number will be given during class; not listed here for security purposes. ) Pronouns: He/him - Last updated: September 18, 2023 - Course Description From videos of insurrectionists storming the US Capitol, to satellite images of potential mass graves in Ukraine, to networks of disinformation websites from Russian state-affiliated media, to eyewitness accounts of police brutality shared on social media, journalists have access to more information today than ever before. A new generation of reporters is already using this information to conduct compelling, award -winning investigations. OSINT reporters at the New York Times, BuzzFeed News, and the Washington Post, for example, have shared in several Pulitzer Prizes and other major awards. Now, for the first time, USC Annenberg is offering an interdisciplinary course in this groundbreaking form of investigative reporting. Students will learn this powerful form of journalism and online investigation, giving them vital skills that will put them at the cutting edge of journalism, and equip them to enter other fields such as human rights and law enforcement. This course will introduce students to the practices of open -source investigations in journalism. Students will learn how to leverage publicly available sources of online information to uncover stories, verify claims, and investigate complex issues. The course will cover a range of tools and techniques used in open-source investigations, including social media monitoring, website forensics, and geospatial analysis. Students will also learn about ethical, legal, security, and preservation standards that set the foundations for effective open-source research. The course will be taught through a combination of case studies, in -class experimentation of tools and techniques, and practical, hands-on work to provide students with a thorough grounding in open-source investigations. With guidance from the instructor, students will have the opportunity to put their online investigative skills to practice by launching their own investigations and supporting real-world projects by external journalists and newsroom partners. Students will also develop and gain access to a larger community of professionals, resources, and industry experts such as open-source reporters from organizations such as the New York Times, the Washington Post, Bellingcat, and Human Rights Watch. Prerequisite Students must have taken JOUR 539 (Introduction to Investigative Reporting) or have journalistic experience that demonstrates the skills taught in JOUR 539. Students from outside the School of Journalism can apply for entry into the course. They will be evaluated based on the skills that are relevant to OSINT reporting, such as computer programming or the ability to translate 2D photos and videos into 3D models.
